p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for twenty two months, and the target burn is February 18, 2063.
When Greaves aired AR 2207's closure record, Sam had already called the crew, Frances, Bea, Hana, and the board, and he gave Greaves the facts on the record.
The readiness board will choose in December between flying the valve with a software workaround and replacing it by spacewalk, and the workaround's ground runs are its evidence.
A partner government pulled sixteen million dollars after an election, and launch 3, with the Breather and its lander, flies in November.
Then Wendell collapsed at the console during a night ground run, and though he's all right, he says this is his last campaign: he'll see it to December, and then he's done.
Wendell Price. Test conductor, seventy one.
Arlo Dunn. The stand's night technician, thirty one, from Limon.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Yusra Haddad. Halcyon's commander, and now the product owner of the flight software backlog.
New in this chapter: Lorna Whitcombe.

Friday, November 10. 4:15 AM. The chair by the bed was the kind hospitals buy because it folds out, and it didn't fold out, and Sam had stopped trying at three. Wendell was asleep with his mouth open and his hearing protection still around his neck. A nurse had tried to take it off him at midnight. He'd woken up long enough to say no.

His canvas jacket was on the hook behind the door. The pockets were worn through at the corners, and one of them had a pencil in it, and a run sheet from the blockhouse folded in quarters. Sam unfolded it standing up.

WORKAROUND GROUND RUN THU NOV 9 2062 W. PRICE, TC. SOAK 1 START 1700. SOAK 2 START 2030. CONDITIONING CYCLE BEFORE EACH CLOSE. MOIV-2 CLOSED AT CUTOFF. SOAK 1. CYCLE 1 OK. 2 OK. 3 RIPPLE 2 MS AFTER LIFT, UNDER LIMIT. 4 OK. 5 OK. 6 OK. SOAK 2. CYCLE 7 OK. 8 OK. 9 RIPPLE 2 MS AFTER LIFT, UNDER LIMIT. 10

Cycle nine had a tick beside it, in pencil, pressed hard enough to dent the paper. Cycle ten had a number and nothing after it. Sam folded the sheet back along its creases and put it where it had been.
At 4:40 Wendell opened his eyes and looked at the ceiling and said, without turning his head, The shoebox is in the truck. Truck's at the stand.
Bring the truck. Leave the box in it. They're mine. Then he went back to sleep, as if that had been the only thing on his list.

Arlo met Sam at the stand gate at 5:30 with two coffees, and they drove out together on the gravel in the dark. Wendell's truck was where he'd left it, nose to the blockhouse wall, with the window down an inch the way he always left it so the cab wouldn't fog. The shoebox was on the passenger seat with its rubber bands on, and a thermos on top of it like a paperweight. Sam drove it back to Byers and put the keys under the mat and didn't open the box.

On the way back he came past the high bay. The countdown clock over the doors said 100. It had said three figures since the day he got the job, and he hadn't thought about what it would look like when it didn't.

What he did think about, all the way in on I-70 with the sun coming up behind him, was the thing Wendell had stood up at 10:52 to look at, the second before he fell. Nobody knew what it was. Wendell knew. It was in his head with everything else, the ripples and the frost and the sound a seat made when it was lying, and his head had just spent four hours on a monitor in Aurora.

Saturday, November 11. There was an envelope in the mailbox, in green ink, postmarked Golden, and it said S. OKAFOR. Inside it, smaller, folded in half, was another one, and it said, on the front, FOR W. IF HE WANTS IT.
Ruth's Console Log, page twelve: Ask why.

Ruth's console log, 217 days after launch. oh six thirty, federal building. snow. same bench as september. oh seven hundred, board, week 18. my testimony, day 3. oh eight fifteen, counsel for the board: the poll. prop took a second before go. what was the second. oh eight sixteen, I don't know. I didn't ask. oh nine hundred, October 18 2034. why two retests the same morning. told them it was what we had time for. true. thirteen thirty, wendell. 41 minutes. thirteen forty, he said the retests ran warm. frost off the body by 0650. cycle 3 was the only cold one. thirteen forty one, he said he told me. he said nobody can tell from two retests the same morning. I heard a number. 500. I never asked him why 500. thirteen fifty five, clerk read it back. first time it was written down anywhere. sixteen hundred, hall. asked him why he never wrote it up. he said it wasn't a finding. it was how the valve looked. sixteen oh two, asked him about the second. he looked at the snow. said ask me again sometime. seventeen thirty, L plus 217. a card for the binder. ask why.
The card is still taped inside the front cover. You'll have seen it if you've held the binder. I wrote it with the clerk's pen, because mine was in my coat, and the clerk wanted it back.

Here's what page twelve is. For fifteen months a man I'd worked beside every day knew that the two clean retests I'd leaned on were run on a warm valve. He'd said so, in his way. He'd said nobody could tell anything from two retests the same morning, and he'd asked for five hundred cold cycles on the shelf valve, and I wrote down the five hundred and never asked him where it came from. To him the reason was obvious, because he'd watched the frost come off the valve body at ten to seven. To me it was a number a test conductor wanted. It took a federal investigation board and the board's clerk to get it onto paper, and by then there was nobody left to tell it to who could do anything with it.

A philosopher named Michael Polanyi wrote, in 1966, that we can know more than we can tell. I read that in 2037 and put the book down for a week. This chapter is about the part people know and can't easily tell, and how you get it out of one head and into others before the head goes home. It's also about the other kind of handing over. That's when the thing you built goes to the people who'll run it, and you have to let go of it properly.

How the exam asks it. When a key person's know-how is at risk, the PMI answer starts by identifying what knowledge the project critically needs, then uses methods that move tacit knowledge between people. A document dump on the way out the door is the distractor.

The PMBOK Guide puts this inside the Governance domain, in a process called Manage Project Knowledge, section 2.1.6.6. It's short, and it's right. Knowledge comes in two kinds. Explicit knowledge can be codified: written in words, drawn, put in numbers. Manuals, procedures, the torque values on a drawing. It's easy to share and easy to store. Tacit knowledge is personal. It's skill and experience and insight, the feel of a thing, and it's hard to say and harder to write.

Two lines in that section are worth carrying around. The first is that codified knowledge lacks context, so even when it's easy to share, people can misread it or apply it the wrong way. A procedure tells you what to do. It rarely tells you what the man who wrote it was afraid of. The second is that an important aim of knowledge management is turning tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge where you can. Where you can. Some of it never turns. That part has to move from person to person.

The exam outline gives you three verbs under P7, help ensure knowledge transfer. Identify the knowledge critical to the project. Gather it. Foster an environment where it can move. The first verb is the one people skip, because it feels slower than the second. It isn't. An expert's head holds nearly fifty years. Your project needs some of it, by certain dates, for certain decisions, in certain other heads. Find that part first, with the expert, and write down who needs each piece and when. Then you'll know what to gather, and how much of a tired man's time it's worth.

How the exam asks it. First step for knowledge transfer: identify which knowledge is critical, with the expert, and who needs it. "Have them write down everything" and "hire a replacement" both skip that step.

Tacit knowledge moves the way it was learned, by being near the work with someone who knows it. Researchers who study this say it takes personal contact, regular interaction, and trust, and none of those come in a binder. The methods have plain names. Shadowing is the learner watching the expert do the real job. Reverse shadowing is the expert watching the learner do it, which is where most of the teaching actually happens. Pairing is two people on the same live work at the same console, trading the controls. A recorded walkthrough is the expert talking through real data or real footage, on camera, so people can replay it. Apprenticeship is all of that stretched over years, toward a skill someone can be signed off on.

The Guide adds storytelling, which it says is particularly good for tacit knowledge, and after action reviews, which come from the Army and ask what happened, why, and what we'd do differently. It also says, fairly, that newer AI tools such as interview bots can help capture both kinds, and it names the risks: sensitive information leaking out, and confident answers that are simply wrong. A transcript is a fine thing to have. It's a record of what a man said. It doesn't hold how he knew it.

Two habits make any of these work. Turn what comes out into something written wherever it will go: if the expert says that when the position signal wiggles and the pressure doesn't, you believe the pressure, that's now a rule, and it goes in the procedure with his name beside it. And check that the knowledge arrived. Have the learners do the thing, blind, against a standard you agreed before they tried. People are kind to each other at the end of a long job. A blind test isn't.

How the exam asks it. For tacit knowledge, choose methods built on working together: shadowing, pairing, mentoring, apprenticeship, storytelling. Written procedures suit explicit knowledge. Verify transfer by having learners perform against agreed criteria.

People who know a great deal usually can't tell you what they know if you ask them that. Ask a test conductor to tell you everything about a valve and you'll get the drawing number and a story from 2031. The knowledge comes out when it's attached to a moment. So ask about moments.

Walk me through the last time this went wrong. What did you look at first? What did you look at that the procedure doesn't mention? When did you know, and what told you? What would make you stop a run that the data says is fine? What's the mistake a new person makes in their first month here? What do you check that nobody asked you to? Each of those questions has a specific answer, and the answers are where the tacit part lives.

Then ask him to show you. Sit beside him on a real run and ask him to say out loud what he's watching, as he watches it. Experts compress. They don't notice the twenty small things they do, because they stopped noticing them years ago. Talking while working makes some of those twenty visible, and the ones that stay invisible are the reason you put a learner in the second chair for weeks instead of an afternoon.

There's a name for the risk you're managing, borrowed from software people: the bus factor, the number of people who'd have to vanish before the work stalls. On most programs a few critical things have a bus factor of one, and everybody knows which ones, and nobody writes it in the risk register because it feels unkind to the person. Write it down. The entry is for the next person who has to read that trace once Wendell's home in Byers, and for the ones who'll ride on what it says.

How the exam asks it. To draw out tacit knowledge, ask about specific events and decisions, and observe the expert doing real work while explaining it. A key person risk belongs in the risk register, with a response such as cross training.

The third verb, foster an environment, is the one I failed. Wendell didn't hide anything from me. I didn't make a room where it would occur to him to say it. He'd been overruled on page three and asked me to note his objection twice. By October he'd learned that his objections were things I noted. So he gave me numbers, because I took numbers, and he kept the reasons, because nobody asked for them.

If you want people to give you what they know, make it safe and make it theirs. Let them choose the place and the time. Record only with their say, and let them review what's kept. Give them credit by name, in the document, where people will see it. And respect what's theirs. The Code is plain about it in 3.3.4: we respect the property rights of others, and it lists documents and data among the things people own. A man's own notebooks, kept for nearly fifty years, on his own time and across four employers, are his. You can ask. You can't take.

And ask why. Not only what the number is. Why that number. What would make you change it. What do you see that I don't. Those questions are free, and they're the whole difference between page four of my log and the page you're reading.

How the exam asks it. To foster knowledge transfer, build trust: the expert's terms, consent to record, review of what's kept, credit, and respect for what they own. Compelling a release form or seizing materials is the distractor.

The other hand off in this chapter is bigger, and it has its own task in the outline, R10, manage project closure: decide the criteria to close the project or phase, validate readiness for transition to the operations team or the next phase, and conclude the closing activities. The Guide's version, in Close Project or Phase, 2.1.6.9, is a long list that comes down to a few ideas. Make sure there's a plan to keep the value going after the project lets go. Transfer the results into operations. Pass on the knowledge. And identify the outstanding risks that have to be accepted, or transitioned to operations.

Readiness for transition is a set of conditions the receiving team agrees to before the day, and then tests, and the date comes after. Have their people been trained, and can they do the job in rehearsal without you? Are the procedures and rules they'll fly by validated, by them? Does every open issue and every residual risk have a named owner on their side, who has accepted it, with the authority to accept it? Where exactly is the line, the minute, when it stops being yours and starts being theirs? If any of those is fuzzy at the handover, it'll be fuzzy at three in the morning on the worst night of their year.

There's one more thing to hand over, and projects almost always forget it: the benefit. A project usually ends before its benefit arrives. The Guide's benefits management plan names the target benefits, when they're expected, how they'll be measured, and a benefits owner who's accountable for monitoring and reporting them after you're gone. It should exist from the start; if it doesn't, write it now, while you still have everyone in one place. If nobody owns the measure, nobody will ever know whether the work did what it was for.

How the exam asks it. Before transition, validate readiness against criteria agreed with the receiving team: trained people, validated procedures, open issues and residual risks with accepting owners, and a benefits owner. Handing over on a date, or marking open issues closed on paper to make the handover look clean, are distractors.
Training the people who'll own it.

The receiving team needs training, and the PMBOK Guide counts on the job training from another team member, mentoring, and coaching as training, alongside the classroom. For a hand off, the most useful training happens in rehearsal. Let the operations team run the thing while your people watch and keep their hands in their laps. Then put failures into the rehearsals that the operators weren't told about, and see what they do. When they can handle what you throw at them without turning around to ask you, they're ready. Before that, they're watching.

The rules and procedures they'll operate under are part of the deliverable, and the receiving team has to own them. A procedure your team wrote and validated is your procedure. A procedure their team has run in rehearsal, found problems in, and signed is theirs. On a ship those are flight rules and flight procedures; on a factory floor they're work instructions; in an office they're runbooks. The principle doesn't change. Whoever will use them at three in the morning has to have tested them at three in the afternoon.

Write the hand off line itself down as a time and a signature. Phases blur. Sometimes both sides think they own the same thing. Sometimes neither does, and that's the dangerous one. A line on paper, agreed by both, with the open items listed on each side of it, takes an hour to write and saves the worst conversation of the year.

How the exam asks it. Readiness for transition is shown by the receiving team performing in realistic rehearsal and owning the procedures they'll use. Your own team's sign off or a delivered document set doesn't show it.

Every project ends by giving people back. Release them on the dates you promised. The Code calls that 2.2.4, we do what we say we will do, and on a long program people plan their lives around the dates in your resource plan: new jobs, a move, a child's school year. Keeping everyone on just in case is a broken promise with a budget line attached. Keep the specific roles operations still needs, named, with each person's agreement, and help everyone else land well.

Recognition matters most at the end, when it can't be mistaken for a bribe to stay. The Guide says recognition and rewards should fit the person and their culture, and that intangible rewards can matter as much as money. That means asking. Some people want a party. Some people want to go home with their thermos. Thank people for the specific things they did, in words they'd recognize.

And when someone on your team is hurt or ill, people come first, which on this program is the oldest rule we have. Follow the medical advice and your organization's fitness for duty process, change the work to fit the person instead of the other way around, and never let anyone do hazardous work alone. Their medical information is theirs. Tell the team what it needs to know to work safely, and not one sentence more. Talk to the person before you decide anything about them. They'll usually tell you exactly what they need, if you let them finish.

How the exam asks it. Releasing team members: follow the resource plan's promised dates, keep only roles still needed with agreement, recognize contributions in ways people value. Keeping everyone "just in case" or letting people drift off are distractors.
I've wondered for twenty seven years what Wendell heard in that second on the poll. He told me to ask again sometime. I haven't. I think I was afraid he'd tell me.

You have a man like him. Everybody does, on every job worth doing, and he's usually older than you and tired and won't say most of what he knows unless you ask in a way he believes. Ask. Then make sure it lands in other people, people who'll still be there when the ship is, and check that it did. Then let him go home.
How the exam asks it. Knowledge transfer is done when the receivers can use it. Check it with a demonstration against criteria set in advance.

Monday, November 13. 6:05 AM. Wendell's truck was at the stand gate when Sam got there, with the engine off and the window down its inch. Wendell was in the blockhouse in his canvas jacket, pouring coffee from the thermos, as if Thursday had been somebody else's.

He had a sheet from the hospital folded in quarters in his shirt pocket, and he handed it over without being asked, which was how Sam knew he'd decided to fight. Discharged Friday afternoon. Low blood pressure, a medication to stop, a cardiology appointment in December. Under restrictions, in a doctor's handwriting: No night work. No working alone. No more than five hours a day, three days a week. Light duty until cleared.

Light duty's a console, Wendell said. I sit in a chair. Tuesday night's run is cycles eleven to twenty, after a long soak, on the test article. That's the run the board's going to read in December. I'd like to be the one who reads it first.

Corinne was in the doorway with her legal pad. Tallgrass's occupational health nurse had called her at seven on Friday: nobody went back on a hazardous operation after an event like that without a fitness for duty review, and the stand at night, with cryogens on it, was a hazardous operation. Garrett had texted Sam at 9:40 on Saturday night. Board's evidence is his read. Get him back on nights. Hana had written something shorter on Sunday. I'd rather lose the run than lose him.

Arlo was at the far bench with his back to all of them, sorting connectors. He'd made the call from the stand on Thursday night and been in the blockhouse door a minute later, and he'd knelt on the floor beside Quinn until the ambulance came.
Around the site, since Friday, the story had gone four ways. It was his heart. It was a stroke. He was retiring. He'd been let go.
Wendell wants to read Tuesday night's run, and the site has four stories going about him. What should Sam do?
Answer. Sit down with Wendell first, then fit his shifts to what the doctor and the nurse allow.
B. Let Wendell run Tuesday night as he's asked, with Arlo at the console beside him.
C. Tell the huddle what the doctor found to end the four stories, and ask everyone to watch him.
D. Send him home for two weeks to rest while Arlo runs the ground tests in his chair.

He takes Wendell out to the truck, where there's nobody, and asks him what he wants. It takes Wendell a while. I want somebody to read that trace who knows what they're looking at. Then I want to go home. So they build it around that. The nurse clears him on Tuesday for days, inside the doctor's hours. Tuesday's run moves to Wednesday at ten in the morning, with the soak started at four by Arlo and a second tech. Wendell sits beside the console and Arlo sits at it. At the huddle Sam says one sentence about it: Wendell was ill on Thursday, he's back on days, and his health is his business. The four stories stop by Friday.

That's a go. Lead the team by solving the problem with the person at the center of it. Follow the medical advice and your safety process, adjust the work to fit, never let hazardous work happen alone, and keep a person's medical details private.
Tuesday, November 14. 7:30 AM. Wendell was in the big room at seven thirty because seven thirty was inside his five hours. He'd brought the thermos.

Everybody wanted something from him, and everybody had written it down. Garrett's email had come in at 6:02 with a subject line in capitals. KNOWLEDGE CAPTURE. GET IT ALL. EVERY PAGE, EVERY RUN, EVERY STORY. Hana wanted his read of every cycle three since 2059, for the root cause team. Commander Yusra Haddad, on the screen from Houston, wanted to know what she'd be looking at on her display at cutoff, and what it would mean. Lorna Whitcombe, who ran the ARA's flight operations and would fly Halcyon after it left, wanted the console calls. Quinn wanted the propulsion poll.

Rafa had a suggestion, and a demo. The ARA had cleared an interview assistant for program use in the spring: you talked, it asked follow up questions, it wrote everything into a searchable record. Quinn watched the demo and wrote SEARCH on her pad in capitals and underlined it.

Wendell listened to all of it. Then he said, to the table, I've got thirty one days and the doctor says I can use about seventy five hours of them. You can have all of it. You can't have all of it by December.
Everyone wants Wendell's time, and he has about seventy five hours through December 15. How should the team use them?
Answer. Work out with Wendell which of what he knows the coming decisions depend on, and who needs it by when.
B. Have him write down everything he knows before December, in his own words, for each team to draw on.
C. Record his whole career with the approved interview assistant, and search the transcript as questions come up.
D. Ask each lead for their questions, and have him answer them in the order they come in.

It takes the morning, with Wendell and Quinn at the whiteboard and everybody else sent out. They work backward from the dates. December 14, the board picks between the workaround and the spacewalk. January 9, the crew launches. February 18, the burn. Then they ask what each of those needs from Wendell's head, and in whose head it has to be by then. It comes to seven lines. Running a cold soak campaign and reading cycle three live: Arlo, by December 15. Telling a seat from ice from a lying sensor on a trace: the crew, Hana, and Lorna's controllers, by January 9. The propulsion poll: Quinn. His read of every cycle three since 2059: Hana's root cause team, before the board. The rest, the Petrel's campaigns and nearly fifty years of notebooks, goes in a column headed LATER, OR NEVER, in Wendell's own hand.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Identify the knowledge critical to the project with the person who holds it: tie it to the decisions and operations it supports, name who needs it, and set the date. Then you know what to gather.

Wednesday, November 15. 10:00 AM. The run was on at the stand, cycles eleven to twenty after a long soak, with Arlo at the console and Wendell in the chair beside it with a headset on. Sam watched from the back of the blockhouse with Quinn.

Halfway through, on the third cycle after the soak, Wendell said, There, and Arlo Dunn, the stand tech learning his console, said, Where? and Wendell didn't answer, because by the time he could have, it was over. The trace on the screen looked like every other trace. Quinn wrote down the time.

Quinn's seven lines from Tuesday were taped to the blockhouse wall above the coffee can. The question now was how. Garrett's office had sent a template, a procedure package, forty headings long. Yusra had asked for the crew to be in the room. Ilse Brandvold, her pilot, had asked a better question in an email Sam read twice: When he says there, what does he see that we don't? Can he teach us to see it, or only to follow the steps? And somewhere in Rafa's backlog, under the autonomy work, there was a line nobody had filled in: what the ship should do if MOIV-1 chattered with nobody aboard.
Wendell had his hours. Five a day, three days a week, until the fifteenth of December.
Ilse asks if Wendell can teach the crew to see what he sees. What should Sam set up?
Answer. Fly the crew in for one long day with him in the sim bay in December, and record all of it.
B. Have him teach Arlo, Quinn and the crew side by side on live runs, recorded with his consent.
C. Have him dictate the forty heading procedure package, and send it to Arlo, Quinn, and the crew to study.
D. Have him teach Arlo at the console on live runs, and pass Arlo's notes to Quinn and the crew.

They build it from his hours. Two mornings a week Arlo sits the console on live runs and Wendell sits beside him, two headsets on the same channel, and Wendell says there out loud before it's over, every time, and then they replay it until Arlo hears it too. Quinn sits the poll with him. Twice the crew comes up from Houston to the sim bay, and Wendell stands behind Yusra and Ilse with a printout of real traces and makes them call each one. Everything's recorded, with his say, and after every session Quinn writes up what came out of it in one page and Wendell crosses out what's wrong. By the second week there's a sentence on the whiteboard in his capitals: IF POSITION WIGGLES AND PRESSURE DOESN'T, BELIEVE THE PRESSURE. Ilse writes it on her kneeboard card.

Exactly right. Tacit knowledge moves through people working together on the real thing: pairing, shadowing, practice with the expert watching. Record it with consent, and turn what can be written into procedure. Teach the people who'll still be there.

Sunday, November 19. 2:00 PM. Byers. Wendell's kitchen had one window and it faced the grain elevator, and he'd put the table under it so he could see the weather coming. Sam had brought the small green envelope. Quinn had brought the recorder, for the sessions Wendell had said yes to, and a folder from Tallgrass legal.

Wendell read Ruth's page with his reading glasses pushed down his nose and his lips moving a little. He read it twice. He stopped at the thirteen forty one line for a long time. Sam knew that one without looking, in her capitals. He said he told me. He said nobody can tell from two retests the same morning. I heard a number. Five hundred. I never asked him why five hundred.
She wrote it down, he said. I always figured she'd thrown that day out. He folded the page along its old crease and put it in his shirt pocket, behind the doctor's note.

Then he talked, for forty minutes, without anybody asking. About frost. The thermocouple sat on the flange, he said, and the flange lagged, so it told you what the valve had been an hour ago. The frost line on the camera told you now. When the frost had climbed past the second bolt on the body, the seat was cold where it counted, and that was the only cycle worth watching. About the sound. A good close was one knock in the headset. A bad one had a shoulder on it, a softer knock a couple of milliseconds behind, and you heard the shoulder before the trace could draw it.
Quinn reached over and pressed the red button on the recorder, and Wendell stopped in the middle of a word and looked at it.

In the legal folder there was a form. KNOWLEDGE CAPTURE RELEASE. ALL NOTES, RECORDINGS, AND MATERIALS PROVIDED BECOME THE PROPERTY OF TALLGRASS AEROSPACE. Under it was a note from Garrett's office asking that the shoebox be scanned and kept in the company archive as program records. The shoebox was on the counter by the sink with its rubber bands on.
And there was the other thing, which Sam had in his pocket on a card in his own handwriting, copied from page ten: PROP ANSWERED FIRST. WENDELL. GO. HE TOOK A SECOND.
Garrett's release form says everything becomes Tallgrass property. What should Sam do at Wendell's table?
Answer. Switch the recorder off for good and let Quinn take notes by hand, then file her notes.
B. Put the form away and let Wendell set his own terms for the recorder and the notebooks.
C. Explain that the recordings and notebooks become program records, and ask him to sign Garrett's release.
D. Ask him now about the second on the Petrel's poll, the one thing nobody else alive knows.

The legal folder goes back in Sam's bag, unopened, under a bag of jerky from the gas station in Bennett. Your house, your rules. You tell Quinn when it's on. You read what she writes and cross out what's wrong. The notebooks are yours. If you ever want copies somewhere, you say where. Wendell looks at him for a while. Then he reaches over and presses the red button himself and finishes the word he was in the middle of. In the car Quinn says he's going to let them scan the 2034 notebook. He told her so while Sam was in the bathroom. He said, she'd want it kept. He meant Ruth. Sam doesn't ask him about the second, then or later.

That's a go. Foster an environment for knowledge transfer: the expert's place and terms, consent to record, review of what's kept, credit, and respect for his property. Trust is what makes tacit knowledge come out.
Decision five. Dates on a page.

Monday, December 4. 8:00 AM. The high bay was empty for the first time since the summer of 2059. All three of Halcyon's modules had left it, and the floor where they'd stood was swept, and the overhead cranes were parked at the far end with their hooks up, like birds on a wire. The last of the three launches had flown in November. Corinne's people were still on the payroll, sixty seven of them, and most of them had nothing left to build.

She had the plan on her legal pad, copied from the merger's resource plan in April, which had given every person a date. Thirty eight people released on Friday, December 15: some to Tallgrass's next program, some to the end of their contracts, eleven to jobs elsewhere that started the week after. Seventeen more on Friday, January 12, once the crew had launched. Twelve kept through Friday, February 23, the sustaining team for departure. She'd told all of them in April, in writing, and again in September.

Garrett's position was in an email with the subject line NOBODY LEAVES. Keep all sixty seven through departure. The ship was in orbit with a valve nobody understood, and he wasn't going to explain to anybody why the people who'd built it were working somewhere else.

Hale's office in Denver had sent the other position on Friday: the partner committee's answer on the sixteen million was still pending, and the program should cut every cost it could, starting with people it didn't need.

Lorna had sent a third, which was a list of five names from Corinne's team that flight operations wanted on call until the burn, for things only they knew about the stack: two of the propellant loading crew, the harness technician who'd found the revision on the MOIV-1 position sensor, and two people from the Breather's stowage.
Garrett, Hale's office and flight ops each want something different for Corinne's people. How should Sam handle the releases?
Answer. Let each person pick a leaving date between now and February, and fill the gaps as they come.
B. Keep all sixty seven on the program through departure, as Garrett asks, and sort out releases after.
C. Release everyone but the sustaining twelve on December 15, and call back anyone the crew launch needs.
D. Release people on the promised dates, and ask the ones flight ops still needs to stay on.

Corinne walks the list with Lorna on Tuesday morning. Four of Lorna's five names are already in the twelve. The fifth, the harness technician, was due to go on January 12; Corinne asks her, and she agrees to stay through the burn for a retention payment Peg writes up the same day. Everyone else goes on their date. Each person gets a letter from Sam that says what they built, by name and by part, and the ones going to other programs get a call from him to their new manager. Garrett's email gets a two line answer with the resource plan attached. On the 15th, at the high bay door, Corinne shakes thirty eight hands.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Manage resource needs against what the work requires: release people on the promised dates, keep the roles still needed by name and with agreement, and close each assignment properly. Doing what you said you'd do is the whole of the commitment.
Decision six. What the crew needs.

Tuesday, December 5. 9:00 AM. The crew's training backlog lived on a board in the sim bay, because Yusra said a thing she could see across a room was a thing she'd actually do. It had grown. Every card on it was somebody's good idea.
Between now and quarantine on December 26 the crew had about a hundred and forty hours left that weren't already spoken for. The cards on the board asked for two hundred and three.

Some of it was obviously theirs. The workaround procedure for CR 62-311, both versions, depending on December 14. Rafa's new cutoff displays. Dr. Anjali Rao's own list, which was medical and short. Wendell's sessions, two more in the sim bay, with real traces. Some of it was less obviously theirs. Hale's office had asked for an eight hour media block, for interviews from orbit. Garrett's comms office had asked for a four hour session on the Petrel, with Wendell, for a documentary. Two partners had each sent a cultural briefing.
Mateo Echeverría, the flight engineer, had a card of his own: The whole stage. Every valve. From the drawings. It was sixty hours on its own.
Yusra stood in front of the board with her arms folded. I want all of it. I'm going to live on Mars. I'll have time to read there. I don't have time here.
Yusra wants all of it, and the crew's requests run far past the hours they have. What should Sam do?
Answer. Add every request to the training plan, and have Quinn find the extra sixty three hours.
B. Have Wendell decide what the crew learns about the valve, and leave the rest of the board as is.
C. Cut the valve sessions for the media block Hale's office wants, and rely on the written procedure.
D. Go through the board card by card with Yusra, keeping what the crew will do or decide in flight.

They take the cards down one at a time, all two hundred and three hours of them, and Yusra asks each card the same thing out loud, the way a customs officer would: in flight, what do we do with you, and when? If there's an answer, the card stays, broken down to the task. If the answer is on Mars, it goes in a cardboard box Quinn labels CRUISE in marker. Two hundred days is a lot of reading time. No answer, and it goes back to whoever sent it, with a sticky note from Quinn. The media block becomes one hour. The documentary goes back to Garrett. Mateo's sixty hours become eight, on the valves he'd actually touch, and the drawings go into the cruise box. The board comes to 131 hours, nine under. Yusra initials the bottom corner with a marker. Now it's mine.

Exactly right. Define scope by the work and decisions it has to support, break it down, and get the customer's agreement on what's in and what isn't. On an adaptive backlog, the product owner orders it and parks what can wait.

Wednesday, December 6. 10:00 AM. Flight control at Watkins was a low building with a wind sock, and the wind sock was straight out. Lorna met Sam at the door with two coffees and the face of someone who'd been handed a lot of ships.

She'd flown four cargo landers to the Moon's south pole for the ARA, and one of them had landed on its side and kept working, and she had a photograph of it on her console. Her twelve controllers would fly Halcyon from the minute the program let go of it until it reached Mars, and then support the crew on the ground there. They'd sat in on every sim since August. They'd never owned anything on it.

The plan said the hand off was at departure plus twenty four hours, on February 19, after the burn and the first checkout. It didn't say much else. Garrett wanted the hand off at cutoff, the minute the burn ended, so Tallgrass's name would be on the burn and not on anything after it. Lorna had asked for the document package by January 1. I'll read it over the holidays and tell you what I think.

On the program's issue log there were nineteen open items. Most were small. One wasn't: I-62-117, MOIV-1 on orbit, root cause open, response to be chosen December 14. There was also the autonomy mode, which the board had kept as an option since last year, and which nobody in Lorna's building had been trained to command.
Lorna put her coffee down. Tell me what I'm taking, Mr. Okafor. All of it. Including the parts you'd rather I found out about later.
Garrett wants the hand off at cutoff. Lorna wants to know everything she's taking. How should Sam set it up?
Answer. Close the program's open issues before the hand off, and give flight ops a clean ship to start.
B. Keep the program team flying the ship through the cruise, with flight ops shadowing until arrival.
C. Agree with Lorna now on what must be true before flight ops takes the ship, then test it in sims.
D. Hand flight ops the full document package on January 1, and let them say when they're ready.

They write it on her whiteboard that afternoon, in her words, and she signs it, and so does he. Nine conditions. Every controller certified on the Halcyon procedures in three integrated sims, two of them with failures Lorna picks and doesn't tell anyone about. The flight rules and the cutoff procedure, including the rule that a pressure reading outranks a position reading at cutoff, validated by her people in the sim, not by Tallgrass's. Every one of the nineteen open items listed with an owner on her side who has read it and accepted it, or a reason it stays with the program until the burn. I-62-117 stays where it belongs, with the board, which accepts the risk or doesn't on the 14th; Lorna's people own the procedure for living with whatever it decides. The hand off line itself, written as a time and a signature: departure plus twenty four hours. If any of these isn't true on the nineteenth, I won't take it, she says, and you won't want me to.

That's a go. Validate readiness for transition against criteria the receiving team agrees in advance: trained and certified people, procedures they've validated themselves, every open issue and residual risk with an owner who accepts it, and a clear hand off point.

Friday, December 8. 7:30 AM. It had been Wendell's idea, which surprised nobody who knew him. On Thursday he'd picked twenty cycle threes out of the archive himself, from 2059 to last week, and stripped the dates and the run numbers off them. Six were real, by his reading: the seat doing the thing nobody could explain. The rest were ice, or the stand, or a sensor telling a lie. He'd sealed his answers in an envelope and given it to Hana.
Three people had read them blind. Arlo and Quinn had been beside him for three weeks of live runs. Yusra had had her two sessions in the sim bay and a printout she'd marked up on the plane.

The criteria were on the board, written on Wednesday with Lorna and Hana, before anybody had read a trace: miss no real event, make no more than two false calls, get at least ninety percent of the twenty right.

Hana had opened Wendell's envelope at six on Thursday evening and laid the three answer sheets beside it. Arlo had found five of the six real ones, and called one of the others real when it wasn't. Quinn had found all six, and called three of the others real. Yusra had found all six, and called only one of the others real.
Arlo had missed number eleven, from October 2059. He'd sat in front of the trace for a long time on Thursday, Hana said, and then called it ice.
Garrett had seen the scores by eight. 90 percent is an A. Sign him off. Wendell's done on the 15th. Arlo hadn't said anything to anyone. He'd asked Hana for trace eleven back.
Arlo scored ninety percent on the blind reads, and Garrett says sign him off. What's Sam's best move?
Answer. Sign Arlo off as test conductor on his ninety percent, and let Wendell finish on the 15th.
B. Have Wendell check Arlo's calls by phone from Byers through January as a second opinion.
C. Set one bar for all three at eighty five percent correct, and sign off whoever clears it.
D. Keep the criteria as written, and have Wendell take Arlo through trace eleven before a retest.

Wendell takes Arlo through trace eleven on Saturday morning, inside his five hours, at the kitchen table in Byers. It was the frost. The camera had been fogged on that run in 2059, and the thermocouple on the flange said cold, and the valve wasn't. You read it right off what you had. What you had was wrong. When the camera's out, you don't call it. That goes in the procedure too. On Tuesday Hana gives Arlo and Quinn twenty new traces. Arlo gets twenty. Quinn gets nineteen, one false call. On Wednesday morning, before the last run, Wendell signs Arlo off as test conductor on the back of the sheet, in pencil, and then again in ink when Corinne brings the form.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Knowledge transfer is verified by the receivers performing against criteria set beforehand. When the test finds a gap, close it with the expert and test again. The criteria are what make the result trustworthy.
Saturday, December 9. 11:00 AM. Quinn came into the program room on a Saturday with two coffees and put one in front of Sam, which was the order things had always gone in between them.

She'd been named the countdown lead in November, in a memo from the program that the board had noted without comment. She'd run every rehearsal since. She ran them well. She sat down and put both hands flat on the table, which Sam had learned two years ago meant the news was bad, or that she was about to ask for something.

I've never run a real one, she said. I've run eleven rehearsals and I know the book cold. I don't know what it's like when it's the real thing and somebody's voice changes on the loop. Wendell does. He's leaving. Delphine's run forty two from her pad. And Ruth ran them for twenty two years. She looked at the coffee. I'm not asking for help. I'm asking who I should ask.
Garrett, who'd heard about the rehearsals from somebody, had already suggested that she shadow one of his vice presidents, who had once run a satellite launch for a different company.
Quinn asks who she should ask before her first real count. How should Sam answer her?
Answer. Ask Ruth to mentor her privately, with her twenty two years of running countdowns.
B. Ask her what she wants to learn, then line up Delphine and an hour with Wendell.
C. Mentor her yourself for an hour every evening between now and launch.
D. Tell her she's ready to run the count on her own, after eleven clean rehearsals.

He asks her first what she wants out of it. She's got a list, because she's Quinn, and it's on the back of a rehearsal script: hear a voice change on the loop and know what to ask; call a hold early and not apologize for it; run a poll when somebody takes a second. Delphine says yes on the phone before he's finished asking: an hour every Thursday until launch, on the loop with Quinn for two of the Cape rehearsals, and her number for the night of. Wendell says yes to one hour, on the poll, on the 11th. Ruth's name doesn't go on the list, and Quinn doesn't ask why; the board will judge the count. Garrett's vice president gets a polite note. On Thursday Delphine tells Quinn the first thing she ever learned about a countdown. The clock's the only thing in the room that isn't scared.

Exactly right. Organize and act on mentoring opportunities: start with what the person wants to learn, match mentors who have it, agree goals and a cadence, and watch for conflicts of interest, here a mentor who sits on the board that judges the count.
Decision ten. Air, not a date.

Monday, December 11. 8:15 AM. There was a new poster on the wall of flight control. Lorna's controllers had made it themselves over the weekend, and it was good, in the way of things made by tired people who like each other: Halcyon in silhouette, the wind sock, and in big letters, LAUNCH FEB 18. DELIVER THE BREATHER.

The engineering packet from Ares Station had come in overnight, from Chiamaka Okonkwo's Breather operations team, in the format they always used. Item four was a question. Who on Earth measures whether this worked, and when do they stop measuring? Our people are asking what success is. Most of them think it is breathing.

The families' newsletter that week had the countdown on its front page. Rafa's team had a sprint goal on their own whiteboard that ended at cutoff. The crew's training board ended at quarantine. Yusra's initials were on its bottom corner. Each picture was true, and each one stopped where somebody's job did.
Lorna had read item four before Sam had. They're right, you know. My poster ends at departure. My job doesn't end until they're breathing. Nobody's ever written down who decides that they are.
Chiamaka's team asks how anyone on Earth will know the Breather worked. What's the right move?
Answer. Get flight ops, the crew and the station to agree on what success is and who measures it.
B. Ask the ARA's public affairs office to write a vision for the teams, the partners, and the public.
C. Leave flight ops its departure poster as its goal, and let the station set its own measure.
D. Write one program vision statement yourself, and send it to every team and the station.

It takes two sessions, because the station is fifteen minutes away by light and answers a day later. Quinn writes the draft with Lorna, Yusra, and Rafa in one room, and sends it up in the packet, and Chiamaka's team sends it back marked up. What comes out is half a page. The benefit is the station's oxygen reserve rising instead of falling, measured on Ares Station, every sol, from the day the Breather starts until ninety sols after. The owner is someone on the station, named by the station before the crew leaves Earth, who reports to the board through the director's packet. Assumptions and risks underneath, in a list. Lorna's controllers take their poster down on Wednesday and put it back up with one line added under it in marker, in a controller's block capitals: AND THEN 90 SOLS OF AIR.

That's a go. Help ensure a shared vision with key stakeholders, find the root cause of the misunderstanding (each group's picture ended with its own job), and keep it current at transition by making the benefit measurable, with an owner and a timeframe.
Tuesday, December 12. 5:40 AM. The kitchen in Aurora, with the coffee maker going. One way fifteen minutes and eight seconds.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4200. One way, 15 minutes 8 seconds. Margin, 259 days. Hi, Dad. Log fifty four. Today's sol is a round one, and I like a round number. Okonkwo says that's the most engineer thing about me. The crew's files came up in the packet. The parts we're allowed. Brandvold keeps bees in Montana and has a pilot's license for everything with wings. Echeverría fixed a desalination plant on a ship once, in a storm, and wrote a paper about it that I've now read twice. Dr. Rao has the shortest file and the longest list of what she's bringing, and Malik's already asked if any of it is chocolate. And Commander Haddad. Four kids. I'd been told that, but it's different in the file, where it's a line in a box. I picked her bunk. They let me. It's the one in C ring nearest the galley, which is the loud one, with the pumps under the floor and everybody going past at shift change. People think nobody wants it. I think somebody with four kids at home is going to want to hear people. If I'm wrong she can have mine. Something else. I've been keeping a log since the ration cut. Not this one. A station one, of what we got wrong. Okonkwo calls it the confession book. It's mostly hydroponics and two pages about the galley. I'll read you two, because I think you'll understand them. SOL 3561. RATION CUT. WE TOLD PEOPLE IT WAS TEMPORARY. IT WASN'T. DON'T SAY TEMPORARY. SOL 4013. STACK 3, CLAMP 2. I SAID THE LOOP WAS DRAINED. IT WASN'T. ASK HOW YOU KNOW. THEN ASK AGAIN. That's the whole method. Write the date, write what happened, write what you'll do. Keep it short so people actually read it. I don't know where I got it from. It feels like something you'd do. The sleeve's off. The skin's pink and shiny and Malik says my arm looks like a pear. Ribs are fine. Mom's watch is on my wrist, still on Aurora time, so I know it's five in the morning there and you're watching this with the coffee maker going. Mine says 259, and the ship gets here on day 268. Same minus nine. The board's number is still minus two. The other place is coming along. Still not in my number. Tell Quinn I said hi. I've never met her and I feel like I have. Log fifty four. Ada out.

He played the two entries again. Then he got up and went to the shelf where he kept Ruth's pages in a manila folder, and took out page one, and laid it on the table beside the tablet, and looked from one to the other. A date. What happened. What you'd do. Capitals. Ada had never seen a page of Ruth's in her life.

At nine, at Watkins, the program's own lessons learned register had three hundred and forty two entries in it. Quinn had kept it since March of last year, started the week the plan was baselined, and most of it was good and none of it had left the building. The ARA's closeout instructions said lessons were due ninety days after the end of the mission.

Two of the entries were new, from Wendell's sessions. The ARA's standard test procedure for crit 1 valves didn't ask anyone to record the thermal state of the valve on a repro attempt. And it didn't ask anyone to record the accelerometer channel, only to listen to it, so the knock and the shoulder Wendell had heard since the Petrel had never once been kept.
New lessons from Wendell's work are in the register. What should Sam do with them?
Answer. Write each lesson up with the names of the people involved, for the agency's review.
B. Hold lessons for the closeout retrospective in March, when the team has hours for them.
C. Send the two valve lessons now to the ARA office that owns the crit 1 procedure.
D. Keep building the register, and send it complete to the ARA with the final report.

Quinn finds the owners by Wednesday: the ARA's test standards office owns the crit 1 valve procedure. Sam sends the two entries with the evidence, Wendell's name beside each, and a sentence asking for a change. The office calls on Thursday. Both changes go into the next revision: record the frost line and the flange temperature on every repro attempt, and record the accelerometer channel on every crit 1 valve test. The ARA's next crit 1 valve test, a cargo lander's in March, will be the first to use them. The register goes on the agenda of the Monday program meeting, ten minutes, two entries a week, to a named owner. On Tuesday night Sam asks Ada, in his reply, whether her station's lessons could go into the register. Not her log. Her lessons. She answers in a packet note the next afternoon, and sends twelve.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Use lessons learned while they can still change something: route them to the owners of the organizational process assets they'd change, ask for the update, and make the register part of how the team works every week.

Wednesday, December 13. 9:00 AM. The last ground run of the workaround campaign, cycles thirty one to forty, after the longest soak yet. The board's data closed at five that afternoon, for the session in the morning.
Arlo had the console, signed off that morning in ink, at the bench, before the run. Wendell had the chair beside it, and the headset.

Wendell's contract ended on Friday, the day after the board. He'd picked it himself. The board's docket notice for the 14th had asked for the test conductor of record to attend, and Wendell said he'd go to that and then he'd go home.

Tallgrass's communications office wanted an event. Garrett's office had ordered a plaque, with a pronghorn on it, and asked Greaves's producers whether they'd like to film the presentation at the Friday all hands, which they would. Corinne had a checklist: his badge, his tools, the stand's records, the console log, his contract, his last timesheet. Hana had written something on a card and hadn't given it to anybody.
Wendell, asked by Quinn on Monday what he'd like, had said he'd like to go home with his thermos.
Garrett ordered a plaque, and Wendell wants to go home with his thermos. How should Sam handle the send off?
Answer. Keep his contract open on standby through departure, in case the valve does anything.
B. Let him leave quietly as he wants, and have Corinne close out his records the week after.
C. Ask Wendell how he wants his last shift marked, and close out his role with him before Friday.
D. Hold Garrett's plaque ceremony at the Friday all hands, with Greaves's crew there to film it.

He wants the last run with Arlo in the chair and himself beside it, and coffee from the thermos after, in the blockhouse, with whoever's on shift. So that's what it is. Cycle thirty three has a ripple on it and Arlo says there before it's over, and Wendell says, Yep, and nothing else. Afterward Corinne walks the checklist with him at the bench, and he hands over the badge himself, and the stand's records go into the archive with his name on the cover sheet as test conductor of record, 2059 to 2062. Hana gives him her card. Sam gives him a letter that says what he did, by date: the third attempt he asked for in September 2059, the notebooks he carried into Room 4, the night shifts of this autumn, the shoulder and the frost, written into a procedure with his name on it. Garrett's plaque goes to Byers in the mail. Wendell puts it in the truck, face down, next to the shoebox.

Exactly right. Close a person's role as part of closing the phase: recognize them in the way they value, for specific contributions, release them on the agreed date, and finish the records, handover, and acknowledgments with them, before they go.

Wednesday, December 13. 11:30 PM. The kitchen in Aurora. He'd come home at eight and eaten standing up, and then sat down at the table with Ruth's twelve pages in their folder and the tablet beside them, and hadn't opened either.

The last run had ended at 1:50 PM, inside Wendell's five hours. Cycle thirty three had had its ripple, and Arlo had said there before it was over, and Wendell had said yep. Afterward there'd been coffee from the thermos in the blockhouse, in paper cups, for nine people, which was more than the thermos held, and somehow it had held it.

Ilse's kneeboard card was in Sam's inbox, photographed, because she'd wanted him to see it. Eleven lines in her handwriting, the first one in Wendell's capitals, copied exactly: IF POSITION WIGGLES AND PRESSURE DOESN'T, BELIEVE THE PRESSURE. The crew would carry it to orbit on January 9 and to Mars after that. The shoulder and the frost weren't in one head anymore. They were in theirs, and Arlo's, and Quinn's, and that was the point.

Arlo's sign off sheet was in the file, pencil and then ink. Trace eleven was taped to the blockhouse wall above the coffee can, with a line under it in Arlo's writing: CAMERA OUT, DON'T CALL IT. Ada's twelve lessons had come up in that afternoon's packet note, and they were in the register under her own name, with the confession book's two entries on top.

Five weeks of handing things to other people. Most of it, he thought, had landed where it was supposed to. He'd been a crew chief long enough to know that a hand off you feel good about is the one you check twice.
At 11:40 the tablet chimed the plain chime it used for work. The board's docket system had run its batch.

The board's docket for Thursday, December 14, at nine. Item one, CR 62-311: the choice for I-62-117, the workaround or replacement by spacewalk. Sitting: the chair, R. Calder, and four others. The board asks the test conductor of record and his successor to attend in person. Submissions: the program's data package, closed at five on Wednesday, and from Tallgrass Aerospace, request for waiver 62-14, filed at 6:12 that evening.
He hadn't filed a waiver. He opened it.

REQUEST FOR WAIVER 62-14 CRITICALITY 1 ITEM OPEN AT FLIGHT READINESS. ITEM: I-62-117 AR 2207. MOIV-1, HALCYON DEPARTURE STAGE. REQUEST: FLY MOIV-1 WITH THE CR 62-311 WORKAROUND. ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION TO CONTINUE DURING CRUISE. REPLACEMENT BY SPACEWALK NOT REQUIRED. RATIONALE: GROUND RUNS WITH THE WORKAROUND NOMINAL. THE PROGRAM JUDGES THE RISK ACCEPTABLE. PREPARED BY: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF EXECUTIVE, TALLGRASS AEROSPACE. SIGNATURE: BLANK. S. OKAFOR, PROGRAM MANAGER

His name was typed under the line, in the board's capitals, the way the board wrote everybody's. The word nominal sat in the rationale like it had been there all along. Ruth would read it on the bench at nine, with a green pen. Wendell would be sitting in the second row, with her page in his shirt pocket, and the frost and the knock he'd taught them to watch for were all through the runs it called nominal.
At 11:52 Garrett texted. Sign it in the morning. Board will land there anyway. This just makes it ours.

Sam put the tablet face down on the table. On the counter by the door, under his keys, the envelope he'd addressed to Ruth in February was where it had been since, with the photocopy in it, still unsealed. He didn't open that either.
